reference.source: Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies / HLH consensus (Histiocyte Society) guidance
clinicalPearls: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome from inherited defects in lymphocyte cytotoxicity, typically presenting in infancy
Causative genes include PRF1 (perforin), UNC13D (Munc13-4), STX11 and STXBP2, all required for cytotoxic granule delivery and killing
The clinical picture is prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly and progressive cytopenias affecting two or more lineages
Characteristic laboratory findings are very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia, raised soluble interleukin-2 receptor and low or absent natural killer cell function
Haemophagocytosis on bone marrow examination supports but is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis
Central nervous system involvement with irritability, seizures or cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis is common and prognostically important
Treatment is HLH-directed immunochemotherapy to control the hyperinflammation followed by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which is required for cure of the genetic forms
reference.pathophysiology: Familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis results from inherited defects in the machinery that cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells use to kill infected or activated target cells. Genes such as PRF1, which encodes the pore-forming protein perforin, and UNC13D, STX11 and STXBP2, which govern the docking, priming and fusion of cytotoxic granules, are required for delivery of the lethal granule contents. When cytotoxicity fails, activated lymphocytes cannot eliminate their targets or contract the immune response, so persistent antigenic (often viral) stimulation drives relentless activation of T cells and macrophages. The resulting cytokine storm, with excessive interferon-gamma and macrophage activation, produces the fever, cytopenias, organ infiltration and haemophagocytosis that define the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary (acquired) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis triggered by infection, malignancy or rheumatic disease
Macrophage activation syndrome complicating systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or Still disease
X-linked lymphoproliferative disease and other genetic HLH-predisposing immunodeficiencies
Severe congenital or acquired infection with cytopenias and organomegaly
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin, fasting triglycerides and fibrinogen
Natural killer cell function assay and flow cytometry for perforin and CD107a degranulation
Bone marrow aspirate looking for haemophagocytosis
Genetic testing of PRF1, UNC13D, STX11 and STXBP2 and related HLH genes
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and neuroimaging to assess central nervous system involvement
redFlags: Rapidly rising ferritin with worsening cytopenias and coagulopathy
Neurological deterioration such as seizures, altered consciousness or cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis
Multi-organ dysfunction with hepatic failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation
Recurrence of hyperinflammation implying an underlying genetic cause requiring transplantation
reference.prognosis: Untreated familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is almost uniformly fatal, but prompt control of hyperinflammation with immunochemotherapy followed by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the chance of long-term survival, with outcome strongly influenced by early diagnosis and the extent of central nervous system involvement.
pitfalls: Attributing the picture to sepsis and missing the diagnosis while the patient deteriorates
Waiting for haemophagocytosis on marrow before acting, when it may be absent early and is not required for diagnosis
Failing to distinguish primary genetic HLH from secondary causes, which alters the need for transplantation
Overlooking central nervous system disease that requires directed therapy
references: Histiocyte Society HLH diagnostic and treatment guidelines
management: Prompt immunochemotherapy to suppress hyperinflammation with etoposide and dexamethasone on an HLH-94/2004 protocol, with ciclosporin
Interferon-gamma neutralisation with emapalumab for refractory disease
CNS-directed therapy with intrathecal methotrexate and corticosteroid where there is neurological involvement
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the definitive curative treatment
Identify and treat any triggering infection, such as Epstein-Barr virus, using rituximab for EBV-driven disease
Intensive supportive care with antimicrobial prophylaxis and blood-product support
Genetic counselling with testing of PRF1, UNC13D, STX11 and STXBP2 and cascade family screening
Urgent referral to a specialist immunology and transplant centre
